California has a history of rewarding those willing to look beneath the surface. Gold in the rivers and oil beneath the ground. Each resource triggered a rush of capital, but the enduring value was rarely created by the natural resource alone. Much of it accrued to those who supplied the tools, financed the claims, and built the roads, railways, and pipelines that turned discovery into an economy. Investment in that infrastructure transformed what lay beneath the ground into an asset, a stream of cash flows, and ultimately something a balance sheet could capture. Two of the greatest capital rushes in American history were financed from this same corner of the California map. In 1849, the resource was gold, the tool was a pan. In 1892, when Edward Doheny sank the first commercial well in what is now downtown Los Angeles, the resource was oil and the tool was a derrick. In both cases, the natural resources sparked the rush, but the infrastructure around it determined how value scaled. The third rush, being financed as we write, is drilling for something more abstract but no less physical. It is drilling for compute. The value was never just the resource; it was often the pipes that moved it.

This is where our provocation begins. The scale of ambition embedded in the AI capex cycle requires a fuel supply that no single financing channel has ever delivered on its own. Hyperscaler balance sheets can fund part of it. Public debt and equity can fund another part. But the buildout will increasingly require scaled pools of capital such as asset-based finance, private investment grade, infrastructure capital and financing solutions that did not exist five years ago. At the same time, the buildout is also catalyzing innovation in the financing itself. New structures are emerging in real time as capital markets adapt to these assets, revenue streams, and risks. Even as we pen this note, leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic and other frontier labs have highlighted the importance of pacing in advanced model development, a reminder that the trajectory of AI investment may evolve over time.


To be clear, at KKR we are believers and investors in this ambition and believe the U.S. has a leading role to play. **** But at today's scale and pace of expected investment, we think the availability of capital in the right form may become a live constraint. That is different from saying capital will run out. More broadly, the AI buildout reflects a uniquely powerful combination of technological leadership, deep capital markets, and an ecosystem capable of funding this innovation at scale, all of which reinforce our conviction in continuing to invest behind the theme. The question is not simply whether there is enough capital, but whether there is enough of the right kind of capital, arriving in the right form, at the right price, and with the right structural protections. In our view, the risk today is twofold: that capital becomes constrained, and that the discipline to deploy it fades.


The credit story compounds from there. Diversification is harder than it looks when the same short list of counterparties sit behind the equity book, the debt book, and increasingly the infrastructure supporting both. Power, chips, cooling, land, leases and financing often route back to the same handful of economic actors.


An allocator who believes they are diversified across strategies may ultimately be more diversified across wrappers than end issuers, sectors, or economic drivers. Historical correlations can also provide a false sense of comfort because the AI capex cycle is new. Exposures that appeared uncorrelated in the past may behave differently as they become increasingly dependent on the same underlying theme. Beneath them sits another layer of market plumbing, including securities lending, margin financing, guarantees, pledged collateral, and synthetic structures that can shape how risk transmits when markets move.


Compute as an investable asset class is still emerging, but the capital pattern at play is familiar. Capital tends to follow the strongest growth themes first. Institutionalizing infrastructure, pricing, ownership, and discipline tend to follow. Those are the mechanisms that determine whether a rush becomes a durable market.


This note takes a credit and capital markets lens to the AI buildout and asks three questions in sequence. Please note, the credit lens is undoubtedly different from the equity lens. Our focus is on how this large opportunity is financed, what supports repayment, and how the structure holds when the path changes.
**The Rush** Is there enough of the right capital to finance the ambition being priced today?
**The Field** Where does the interconnection actually reside, and what does that mean for the diversification investors believe they own?
**The Discipline** What financing and underwriting discipline and pace can turn this rush into a durable market as the trajectory evolves, whether through regulation, capital constraints, infrastructure bottlenecks, or a natural slowing in the pace of the cycle?


Our affirmative case sits in the answer to the third question. The financing tools this buildout needs are ones the credit markets have spent more than a decade developing: scaled origination, structural seniority, covenants, collateral analysis, and specialized underwriting. Just as important is the ability to draw on expertise across corporate credit, asset-based finance, private equity, and real assets as the risks increasingly cut across traditional asset-class boundaries. The front-page story is how much compute gets built. The credit story is about who gets paid if expectations change.

## Setting the Scene


Global credit enters this note in a market that reads calmer on the surface than at any other point since the start of the year. Spreads remain within ranges investors have learned to regard as normal. Beneath them, however, dispersion is widening sharply. The compensation for stepping from higher-quality IG into BB credit has compressed toward historical lows, while the weakest parts of high yield are trading at increasingly large premiums to the rest of the market. Part of that resilience reflects a structural change in high yield itself. As we recently discussed in the “[High Yield’s Second Act: What AI Revealed About Credit Quality](https://www.kkr.com/insights/high-yield-second-act) ”, the HY market has quietly migrated up in quality, with a record share of bonds now rated BB and a growing portion of the index secured by collateral. That higher-quality composition has helped the market absorb pockets of stress more effectively. The index says calm, but individual credits, sectors, and financing channels increasingly say otherwise.


The September FOMC meeting reinforced KKR's broader macro expectations. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points as persistent inflation continues to demand attention, while long-term Treasury yields remain elevated. For credit investors, the implication is fairly straightforward: one of the largest capital expenditure cycles in modern history is accelerating at a time when the cost of capital remains high and duration is once again an active source of risk, raising the importance of matching financing structures, asset lives, and expected cash flows.


**EXHIBIT 2: Treasury Yields are Testing Multi-Year Highs**


#### U.S. Treasury Yields Spike


Source: Bloomberg as of September 25, 2026.


We saw a version of that dynamic in software earlier this year with what many referred to as the “SAASpocalypse.” The repricing occurred in a matter of weeks in a corner of the market most allocators considered structurally sound, and software became the largest single detractor from performance across the leveraged finance complex. Yet software represents only about 3% of the roughly $1.5 trillion U.S. high yield market, roughly 13% of leveraged loans, and more than 20% of a corporate private credit market of approximately $1.9 trillion. Importantly, the sell-off was not accompanied by a broad deterioration in underlying fundamentals across the software and services sector, and in direct lending, despite heightened concerns around valuations and redemptions, mark-to-market movement was ultimately limited. The more consequential question is what a true fundamental sell-off could look like across an AI complex that is materially larger, more capital intensive, and more interconnected across public and private markets.


**EXHIBIT 3: Individual Hyperscalers Continue to Tell Independent Stories as Spreads Widen**


#### Investment Grade Ex-Hyperscalers vs Individual Hyperscalers Spreads


Source: JPMorgan US Liquid Index (JULI), Bloomberg, and KKR Credit Analysis as of September 17, 2026.


Move one layer deeper and the compression at the top of the market gives way to something very different. The high yield CCC to B spread ratio has reached an all-time high of 3.5x, with distressed spread levels hovering at ~2,600 basis points versus roughly 200 basis points over for non-distressed high yield .1


This is dispersion in its clearest form, and it is a pattern we have been flagging since the end of 2024. Dispersion rarely announces itself through the index or front door. It shows up in asset selection, portfolio construction, and product exposure.


**EXHIBIT 4: The Software Repricing Still has Room to Recover**


#### U.S. Leveraged Loan Returns vs Software Loans


Sources: PitchBook | LCD; Morningstar; S&P Dow Jones Indices — Data through Aug. 31, 2026.


AI is amplifying that divergence. Technology equipment, software, semiconductors, and data center construction are becoming increasingly important contributors to U.S. fixed investment, while capex across much of the rest of the economy is running at a low-growth or contractionary pace. The result is an unusually concentrated investment cycle, with capital increasingly drawn toward the segment of the economy with the strongest growth narrative. At the same time, the scale is materially larger: AI infrastructure CapEx is projected at roughly $7.6-8T trillion through 2030, while AI-linked exposure could ultimately approach 20% of the investment grade index. As that concentration grows, so too do the linkages across issuers, financing channels, infrastructure, and end markets. 2


The result is a market in which seemingly distinct exposures are increasingly driven by the same underlying economics. That is the environment in which the plumbing gets tested.
